name: Oleyl adapalenate

lead: Oleyl adapalenate (Adapinoid) is a cosmetic ingredient described as a third-generation retinoid and pro-drug of adapalene, positioned for photoaging. The payoff is smoother texture and fewer wrinkles with less irritation than retinol.

It is described as releasing adapalene in the skin, which then signals through retinoid receptors. A 2024 randomized, double-blind 12-week trial of 48 people compared 0.5% oleyl adapalenate cream with 0.5% retinol cream and reported greater wrinkle improvement and better tolerability with oleyl adapalenate.

paras: It is used in over-the-counter-style cosmetic creams aimed at photoaging, as a retinoid alternative for people who find retinol irritating. Results in the trial were measured over 12 weeks.

Little safety research exists beyond the one trial, which reported better tolerability than retinol. As a retinoid pro-drug, people who are pregnant or who react to retinoids may want to check with a clinician.

angle.text: Oleyl adapalenate is a cosmetic retinoid pro-drug that converts to adapalene in skin, aiming for smoother texture and fewer wrinkles with less irritation than retinol. A 2024 trial of 48 people over 12 weeks reported greater wrinkle improvement than retinol.

lead: Oleyl adapalenate (sold as Adapinoid) is described as a third-generation retinoid and a pro-drug of adapalene, formed by joining adapalene to an oleyl group.[1] It is used in cosmetic skincare creams aimed at photoaging, positioned as a retinoid that smooths wrinkles with better tolerability than retinol.[1]

A 2024 randomized, double-blind, 12-week trial of 48 adults aged 35 to 65 compared 0.5% oleyl adapalenate cream with 0.5% retinol cream. Wrinkle severity fell 9.45% with oleyl adapalenate versus 4.11% with retinol, facial redness fell 13.39% with oleyl adapalenate while retinol produced no significant change, and oleyl adapalenate users reported less irritation at every visit.[1][2] The trial was funded by the ingredient's supplier.[2]

paras: The authors describe oleyl adapalenate as a pro-drug of adapalene, a synthetic retinoid, whose ester group is expected to be cleaved to adapalene by epidermal esterases.[2] They report higher lipophilicity than adapalene, which they suggest aids skin penetration, and propose that selective affinity for retinoic acid receptors beta and gamma may explain better tolerability; the study did not test this.[2]

One published trial, a prospective, double-blind, randomized head-to-head study (NCT05778760), compared 0.5% oleyl adapalenate with 0.5% retinol in 48 healthy adults, mostly women with lighter Fitzpatrick skin types, applied nightly for 12 weeks with visits at weeks 4, 8 and 12.[1][2] Thirty-nine completed per protocol. Wrinkle severity, the primary outcome, improved by 9.45% with oleyl adapalenate and 4.11% with retinol, a significant between-group difference. Pigment intensity fell by 3.88% and 3.15% respectively, without a significant difference.[2] Oleyl adapalenate reduced facial erythema by 13.39%, whereas retinol produced no significant change.[2]

At week 12, no oleyl adapalenate users reported itching, stinging or redness, versus 11%, 16% and 21% of retinol users for mild itching, stinging and redness, and no adverse events were reported.[2] The authors list as limitations a single site, 12 weeks of follow-up and mostly light skin types, and note that research on the compound is scarce; the two formulas also differed slightly in oil content, and the study was funded by the ingredient supplier, Actera Ingredients.[2]

timeline.event: Head-to-head trial versus retinol conducted (May to August) in the Sacramento region.[2]
Results of the randomized trial published in Skin Health and Disease.[1]
